items.title: Relational vs NoSQL
items.context: Relational databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL) use fixed schemas, tables, rows, and SQL, with strong support for relationships and joins. NoSQL databases (MongoDB, Redis) trade some of that structure for flexible schemas and horizontal scalability.

questions.prompt: Which type of database enforces a fixed schema with tables, rows and columns?
choices: Key-value NoSQL
Document-based NoSQL
None of them enforce schema
Relational
questions.explanation: Relational databases like MySQL/PostgreSQL require a defined schema up front — tables, columns, and types — and use SQL to query across them.

questions.prompt: Which scenario most favors a NoSQL document database over a relational one?
choices: You need standard SQL reporting tools
You need strong foreign-key constraints
You need strict multi-table joins with strong consistency guarantees
Your data's shape varies a lot between records and evolves quickly
questions.explanation: Document stores like MongoDB shine when your records don't share a rigid, uniform schema and that schema needs to evolve without expensive migrations.

items.title: ACID properties
items.context: ACID: Atomicity (a transaction fully happens or not at all), Consistency (it moves the DB from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (once committed, it survives a crash).

questions.prompt: Which ACID property guarantees a transaction either completes entirely or has no effect at all?
choices: Durability
Isolation
Consistency
Atomicity
questions.explanation: Atomicity means a transaction is all-or-nothing — if any part fails, the whole transaction is rolled back as if it never happened.

items.title: Indexes
items.context: An index is an auxiliary data structure (commonly a B-tree) that lets the database find rows matching a condition without scanning the whole table — at the cost of extra storage and slower writes.

questions.prompt: What does adding an index to a column primarily improve?
choices: Write speed for that column
Guaranteed uniqueness of every column
Data compression
Read/lookup speed for queries filtering or sorting on that column
questions.explanation: Indexes speed up lookups (WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY) on the indexed column, at the cost of extra storage and slightly slower writes since the index must also be updated.

questions.prompt: What is a downside of adding many indexes to a heavily-written table?
choices: Indexes replace the need for a primary key
Every write must also update each index, slowing inserts/updates/deletes
Reads become impossible
Indexes make the schema impossible to change
questions.explanation: Every index has to be kept in sync on every write, so more indexes mean more write overhead — index choice is a read/write trade-off, not a free performance win.

items.title: Normalization & foreign keys
items.context: Normalization organizes relational tables to reduce data redundancy and avoid update anomalies, typically by splitting data into related tables. A foreign key is a column that references another table's primary key, enforcing referential integrity between them.

questions.prompt: What is the main goal of normalizing a relational schema?
choices: Making the schema NoSQL-compatible
Reducing data redundancy and avoiding update/insert/delete anomalies
Making queries run without any joins
Removing the need for primary keys
questions.explanation: Normalization splits data into related tables so each fact is stored once, preventing the inconsistencies that arise when duplicated data is updated in only one place.

questions.prompt: What does a foreign key enforce?
choices: That a column's values are always unique
That a table has no more than one index
That a column's value must match an existing primary key value in another (or the same) table
That a column can never be null
questions.explanation: A foreign key constraint ties a column to a primary key in another table, so the database rejects rows that would reference a record that doesn't exist — referential integrity.

items.title: SQL joins
items.context: An INNER JOIN returns only rows with matches in both tables. A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right (with NULLs where there's no match).

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
choices: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables; LEFT JOIN also keeps unmatched rows from the left table
They always return identical results
INNER JOIN can only join two tables, LEFT JOIN can join more
LEFT JOIN is only valid in NoSQL databases
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN drops rows without a match on both sides; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table regardless, filling in NULLs for any right-side columns that have no match.

items.title: MongoDB & Redis
items.context: MongoDB is a document store — records are JSON-like BSON documents grouped into collections, with a flexible per-document schema. Redis is an in-memory key-value store, commonly used for caching, session storage, and rate limiting because of its speed.

questions.prompt: What is Redis most commonly used for in an application architecture?
choices: An in-memory cache / fast key-value store
Enforcing foreign-key constraints
Full-text document search
Long-term relational reporting
questions.explanation: Redis keeps data in memory for very low-latency access, which is why it's a go-to choice for caching, session stores, and rate limiters rather than primary long-term storage.

questions.prompt: How does MongoDB primarily store records, in contrast to a relational table's rows?
choices: As key-only entries with no value
As fixed-width binary blobs
As spreadsheet-style CSV rows
As JSON-like (BSON) documents with a flexible, per-document schema
questions.explanation: MongoDB groups JSON-like BSON documents into collections; unlike a relational table, different documents in the same collection can have different fields.

items.title: Transaction isolation levels
items.context: Isolation levels trade consistency for concurrency. READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads. READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads. REPEATABLE READ prevents those too but can allow phantom reads. SERIALIZABLE is the strictest, preventing all three at the cost of concurrency.

questions.prompt: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads (reading another transaction's uncommitted changes) but still allows non-repeatable reads?
choices: READ UNCOMMITTED
None of them prevent dirty reads
READ COMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
questions.explanation: READ COMMITTED only ever sees committed data (no dirty reads), but re-reading the same row later in the same transaction can still return a different value if another transaction committed a change in between.

items.title: Connection pooling
items.context: Opening a new database connection is relatively expensive (TCP handshake, authentication, session setup). A connection pool (e.g. HikariCP) keeps a set of open connections ready to reuse, handing one out per request and returning it to the pool when done.

questions.prompt: Why do applications typically use a connection pool instead of opening a new database connection for every request?
choices: It's required by SQL syntax
Pools make SQL injection impossible
It removes the need for transactions
Establishing a new connection is relatively expensive, so reusing a pool of open connections is much faster
questions.explanation: Creating a raw database connection involves network and authentication overhead; a pool amortizes that cost by keeping connections open and handing them out/reclaiming them as requests come and go.

items.title: Replication & read scaling
items.context: Replication keeps copies (replicas) of a database in sync with a primary. Read replicas let an application spread read traffic across multiple copies, scaling read throughput, while writes still go to the primary.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of read replicas in a database architecture?
choices: To permanently replace the primary database
To make writes faster
To scale read throughput by distributing read queries across multiple synchronized copies of the data
To automatically normalize the schema
questions.explanation: Read replicas hold a copy of the primary's data (often with some replication lag) and can absorb read traffic, freeing the primary to focus on writes — a common way to scale a read-heavy workload.

items.title: CAP theorem
items.context: The CAP theorem states that a distributed data system can only fully guarantee two of three properties at once: Consistency (every read sees the latest write), Availability (every request gets a response), and Partition tolerance (the system keeps working despite network splits).

questions.prompt: According to the CAP theorem, a distributed system experiencing a network partition must choose between which two properties?
choices: Normalization and denormalization
Security and durability
Speed and cost
Consistency and availability
questions.explanation: Once a partition happens, CAP says you can't have both full consistency and full availability at the same time — the system must favor one, which is exactly the design trade-off many NoSQL systems make explicit (e.g. 'eventually consistent').

items.title: Denormalization
items.context: Denormalization deliberately reintroduces redundancy (e.g. duplicating a column across tables, or embedding related data) to reduce the number of joins a read-heavy query needs — trading some write complexity and storage for faster reads.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off made by denormalizing a schema?
choices: Slower reads in exchange for guaranteed consistency
It only applies to NoSQL databases, never SQL
Accepting some data redundancy and write complexity in exchange for faster, simpler reads
It removes the need for indexes entirely
questions.explanation: Denormalization duplicates or embeds data to avoid expensive joins on the read path, at the cost of having to keep that redundant data in sync on writes.

items.title: Composite primary keys
items.context: When a row's identity requires more than one column together (e.g. an order-line table keyed by order_id + product_id), JPA models this with either @EmbeddedId (a dedicated embeddable key class) or @IdClass (a separate key class mirrored by @Id fields on the entity).

questions.prompt: How does JPA typically model a primary key made up of more than one column?
choices: By adding a second @Table annotation
Using @EmbeddedId (an embeddable key class) or @IdClass
By marking two unrelated columns @Id with no other configuration
It's not supported; every entity must have exactly one column as its key
questions.explanation: @EmbeddedId wraps the composite key fields in their own embeddable class used as the entity's @Id; @IdClass instead mirrors those fields directly on the entity while pointing to a separate class describing the key's shape — both are standard JPA approaches to composite keys.

items.title: Database views
items.context: A view is a saved, named query that behaves like a virtual table — querying it re-runs the underlying query, and the view itself doesn't store data (unless it's specifically a materialized view).

questions.prompt: What is a database view?
choices: A backup of the database
A type of index
A saved, virtual table defined by a query, which doesn't store its own data
A physical copy of a table refreshed nightly
questions.explanation: A (non-materialized) view is just a stored query definition presented as if it were a table — every time you select from it, the underlying query runs against the real, current data.

questions.prompt: How does a materialized view differ from a regular view?
choices: A materialized view stores (caches) the query's result physically, refreshed periodically, rather than recomputing it on every read
There is no difference
Materialized views only work with NoSQL databases
Materialized views cannot be queried with SQL
questions.explanation: A materialized view actually persists its result set to disk and needs to be refreshed (on a schedule or on demand) — trading some staleness for the speed of not recomputing an expensive query on every single read.

items.title: Query execution plans
items.context: Running EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE) on a SQL query shows how the database intends to execute it — which indexes it will use, in what order tables are joined, and where it expects to scan large amounts of data — the primary tool for diagnosing a slow query.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of running EXPLAIN on a SQL query?
choices: To automatically fix slow queries
To see how the database plans to execute the query — index usage, join order, scan types — for diagnosing performance
To back up the query for later replay
To validate the query's syntax only
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN surfaces the query planner's chosen execution strategy, which is the standard starting point for figuring out why a query is slow — e.g. spotting a full table scan where an index should have been used.

items.title: Database migration tools
items.context: Tools like Flyway and Liquibase version-control database schema changes as an ordered sequence of migration scripts, applying only the ones a given environment hasn't seen yet — keeping dev, test, and production schemas in sync in a repeatable, auditable way.

questions.prompt: What problem do migration tools like Flyway or Liquibase solve?
choices: They handle only data backups, not schema
They version-control and apply schema changes in a repeatable, ordered way across environments
They replace the need for a database entirely
They automatically optimize slow queries
questions.explanation: Migration tools track which schema-change scripts have already been applied to a given database and apply only the new ones in order, so every environment converges on the same schema history instead of drifting via manual changes.

items.title: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking
items.context: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: it checks (often via a version column) at commit time whether anyone else changed the row, and fails the transaction if so. Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely: it locks the row upfront, blocking other transactions from touching it until the lock is released.

questions.prompt: What's the core difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking?
choices: Optimistic locking detects conflicts at commit time (e.g. via a version check); pessimistic locking prevents them upfront by locking the row before use
Pessimistic locking never blocks other transactions
Optimistic locking always requires a distributed lock server
They are two names for the same mechanism
questions.explanation: Optimistic locking lets transactions proceed without locking and only checks for conflicts right before committing (typically via a version number); pessimistic locking instead grabs a lock on the row immediately, making other transactions wait rather than risk a conflict later.

questions.prompt: A row representing limited inventory count is updated very frequently by many concurrent transactions, causing frequent optimistic-locking failures and retries. What locking style might reduce wasted work here?
choices: Denormalize the table further
Add more read replicas
Switch to no locking at all
Pessimistic locking, since it prevents the conflicting access up front rather than repeatedly detecting and retrying after the fact
questions.explanation: Under high contention on the same row, optimistic locking can cause a lot of wasted work from repeated conflict-and-retry cycles; pessimistic locking avoids that by serializing access to the contested row directly, at the cost of some throughput from blocking.

items.title: Full-text search
items.context: Plain SQL LIKE queries scan text linearly and don't understand language (stemming, relevance ranking, typo tolerance). Dedicated search engines (Elasticsearch, Solr) or a database's built-in full-text search features index text specifically for fast, relevance-ranked search.

questions.prompt: Why reach for a dedicated search engine (like Elasticsearch) instead of SQL LIKE '%term%' queries for full-text search?
choices: SQL databases cannot store text at all
Dedicated search engines provide relevance ranking, tokenization/stemming, and far better performance at scale
LIKE queries support fuzzy matching by default
LIKE queries are always faster
questions.explanation: LIKE performs a naive substring scan with no understanding of language or relevance; dedicated search engines index text specifically for search — tokenizing, ranking by relevance, and scaling to large datasets far better.

items.title: GROUP BY and aggregates
items.context: GROUP BY collapses rows sharing the same value in specified column(s) into groups, so aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX can be computed per group instead of over the whole table.

questions.prompt: Which SQL clause groups rows by a shared column value so aggregate functions can be applied per group?
choices: GROUP BY
HAVING
ORDER BY
WHERE
questions.explanation: GROUP BY partitions the result set into groups by the specified column(s), letting aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, ...) compute one value per group instead of one value for the entire table.

items.title: Table constraints
items.context: Constraints enforce rules directly in the database: UNIQUE ensures no duplicate values in a column, NOT NULL requires a value, CHECK enforces an arbitrary condition, and a foreign key enforces referential integrity to another table.

questions.prompt: Which constraint guarantees that no two rows share the same value in a given column?
choices: CHECK
NOT NULL
DEFAULT
UNIQUE
questions.explanation: A UNIQUE constraint rejects any insert or update that would create a duplicate value in that column (or column combination), enforced directly by the database rather than application code.

items.title: Clustered vs non-clustered indexes
items.context: A clustered index determines the actual physical storage order of a table's rows — a table can have only one. Non-clustered (secondary) indexes are separate structures that store a copy of the indexed column(s) plus a pointer back to the real row, and a table can have many of them.

questions.prompt: How many clustered indexes can a single table have?
choices: Only one, since it determines the physical row storage order
One per column
Exactly zero, always
As many as needed
questions.explanation: Because a clustered index physically orders the table's rows on disk according to that index, a table can only be organized that one way — additional indexes on other columns must be non-clustered, pointing back to the clustered order (or a heap) rather than reordering storage themselves.

items.title: Normal forms: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF
items.context: 1NF requires atomic column values with no repeating groups. 2NF (on top of 1NF) removes partial dependencies — every non-key column must depend on the whole composite primary key, not just part of it. 3NF (on top of 2NF) removes transitive dependencies — non-key columns must depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns.

questions.prompt: What problem does moving a table from 2NF to 3NF specifically address?
choices: Duplicate primary keys
Repeating groups within a single column
Transitive dependencies, where a non-key column depends on another non-key column rather than directly on the primary key
Missing foreign key constraints
questions.explanation: 3NF eliminates transitive dependency: if column C depends on column B, which depends on the primary key A, then C indirectly depends on A through B — 3NF says C should instead be moved to a table where B is the key, removing that indirection.

items.title: Isolation phenomena: dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads
items.context: A dirty read sees another transaction's uncommitted changes. A non-repeatable read gets a different value re-reading the same row later in the same transaction, because another transaction committed an update in between. A phantom read gets different rows matching the same WHERE clause on a repeated query, because another transaction inserted or deleted qualifying rows in between.

questions.prompt: What is a "phantom read"?
choices: Reading a row that was deleted before the transaction started
Running the same query twice in one transaction and getting a different SET of rows, because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows in between
Reading uncommitted data from another transaction
A read that never returns because of a deadlock
questions.explanation: Phantom reads are specifically about the row SET changing between two identical queries in the same transaction (new rows appearing or existing ones vanishing) — distinct from a non-repeatable read, which is about a single already-read ROW's value changing.

items.title: Primary key vs unique key vs candidate key
items.context: A table may have several candidate keys — any column (or combination) capable of uniquely identifying a row. One candidate key is chosen as the primary key (never null, exactly one per table). The others can still be enforced with unique constraints, which — unlike a primary key — commonly allow one null value.

questions.prompt: What's the relationship between a table's candidate keys and its primary key?
choices: A candidate key is any column(set) that could uniquely identify a row; the primary key is the one candidate key chosen as the table's official identifier
They are unrelated concepts
A table can have multiple primary keys but only one candidate key
Candidate keys always allow duplicate values
questions.explanation: Every column or combination capable of uniquely identifying a row is a candidate key; the designer picks one of those candidates to serve as the actual primary key, while the rest can still be protected with UNIQUE constraints.

items.title: EXISTS vs IN
items.context: EXISTS checks a subquery for the mere presence of any matching row and can stop as soon as it finds one, often performing better on large subqueries — it also handles NULLs more predictably than IN, which compares against a materialized list of values.

questions.prompt: Why might EXISTS be preferred over IN for a subquery that could return a very large number of rows?
choices: EXISTS can stop as soon as it finds one matching row, rather than needing the subquery's full result list the way IN does
EXISTS only works with numeric columns
EXISTS and IN always perform identically
IN doesn't support subqueries at all
questions.explanation: EXISTS is a existence check that can short-circuit on the first match; IN conceptually needs the full list of subquery results to compare against, which can be more expensive when that subquery returns a large result set — EXISTS also avoids some surprising NULL-comparison pitfalls that IN can have.

items.title: Subquery vs JOIN
items.context: A JOIN is typically preferred when you need columns from both tables in the result. A subquery (especially with EXISTS/IN) is often clearer and can be just as efficient for pure existence/filtering checks where you don't need to select anything from the other table.

questions.prompt: When is a subquery (e.g. with EXISTS) often preferred over a JOIN?
choices: When you only need to filter/check for existence and don't need to select any columns from the other table
When you need columns from both tables in the output
Subqueries are always faster than joins in every case
JOINs cannot be used with WHERE clauses
questions.explanation: If the other table is only being consulted to decide whether a row qualifies — with no need to pull its columns into the result — a subquery (particularly EXISTS) often reads more clearly than a JOIN, without the risk of accidentally duplicating rows that a JOIN could introduce.

items.title: Self-joins
items.context: A self-join joins a table to itself (using two aliases) — the classic example is an employees table with a manager_id column referencing another row's id in that same table, letting you pair each employee with their manager's row.

questions.prompt: What is a self-join used for?
choices: Joining a table to itself, e.g. to pair each row with a related row in the same table (like an employee and their manager)
Merging two databases together
Joining two completely unrelated tables
Automatically indexing a table
questions.explanation: A self-join uses two aliases of the same table so you can relate one row to another row within that table — the employee/manager pattern (manager_id referencing another employee's id) is the textbook example.

items.title: Stored procedures
items.context: A stored procedure is precompiled SQL/procedural logic stored and executed inside the database itself — reducing network round-trips and centralizing shared logic, at the cost of being harder to version, test, and port across database vendors than application code.

questions.prompt: What is a key trade-off of putting business logic in a stored procedure instead of application code?
choices: Stored procedures always run slower than application code
They eliminate the need for any indexes
They can reduce network round-trips and centralize logic in the database, but are typically harder to version, test, and port across database vendors
Stored procedures cannot accept parameters
questions.explanation: Running logic where the data lives can cut down on round-trips and keep certain rules enforced centrally, but that logic becomes tightly coupled to a specific database vendor's dialect and is often harder to unit test and version-control than ordinary application code.

items.title: Database triggers
items.context: A trigger is a procedure the database automatically invokes in response to a specific table event (BEFORE/AFTER INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE) — commonly used for auditing, enforcing complex constraints beyond what a CHECK constraint can express, or cascading side effects.

questions.prompt: What is a database trigger?
choices: A type of index
A manually-run maintenance script
A stored connection pool setting
A procedure automatically invoked by the database in response to a specific table event like INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE
questions.explanation: Triggers fire automatically as a side effect of a data-changing event on a table, commonly used for auditing (logging who changed what) or enforcing rules too complex for a plain CHECK constraint.

items.title: NULL and three-valued logic
items.context: SQL comparisons involving NULL don't evaluate to true or false — they evaluate to UNKNOWN. That's why `column = NULL` never matches any row, even rows where the column actually is NULL; you must use `IS NULL`/`IS NOT NULL` instead, which are specifically defined to test for NULL directly.

questions.prompt: Why does `WHERE some_column = NULL` never return any rows, even for rows where some_column is actually NULL?
choices: NULL is treated as equal to everything
The database automatically converts NULL to 0
Comparisons with NULL evaluate to UNKNOWN rather than true or false, so the row is never included — IS NULL must be used instead
It's a SQL syntax error
questions.explanation: SQL's three-valued logic means any comparison operator applied to NULL yields UNKNOWN, not true — a WHERE clause only keeps rows where the condition is true, so NULL = NULL (also UNKNOWN) never qualifies. IS NULL exists specifically because it tests for the NULL condition directly rather than via a comparison operator.

items.title: Using a ResultSet after its Statement is closed

questions.prompt: What happens when rs.next() is called?
choices: Returns true or false normally
Throws NullPointerException
Returns null
Throws SQLException — the ResultSet is closed along with its parent Statement
questions.explanation: Closing a Statement (or its Connection) implicitly closes any ResultSet it produced. Calling any method on an already-closed ResultSet — including next() — throws SQLException. This is why try-with-resources on Connection/Statement/ResultSet together, in that declared order, is the standard safe pattern.

items.title: PreparedStatement parameter index out of range

questions.prompt: What happens on the second setString() call?
choices: Throws SQLException — parameter index 2 is out of range for this statement
Overwrites the first parameter
Silently ignored
Compile error
questions.explanation: The query has exactly one placeholder (?), so valid parameter indices are just 1. Calling setString(2, ...) references a parameter position that doesn't exist in the prepared SQL, and the JDBC driver throws SQLException ("parameter index out of range") at that call.

items.title: Calling previous() on a forward-only ResultSet

questions.prompt: What happens when rs.previous() is called?
choices: Compile error
Returns false without moving
Throws SQLException — the default ResultSet type is forward-only
Moves the cursor back one row normally
questions.explanation: Statement.createStatement() with no arguments produces a TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY ResultSet by default — its cursor can only move forward via next(). Calling previous(), first(), absolute(), or relative() on a forward-only result set throws SQLException. Getting a scrollable cursor requires explicitly requesting TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE (or _SENSITIVE) when creating the Statement.

items.title: Closing a connection with autoCommit(false) and no commit()

questions.prompt: What happens to the UPDATE when the connection is closed without an explicit commit() or rollback()?
choices: The update is committed automatically on close()
Behavior is driver-defined, but most JDBC drivers roll back an open transaction on close() — the update is typically lost
The connection pool commits it later
Throws SQLException: uncommitted transaction
questions.explanation: With autoCommit(false), you're responsible for calling commit() to make changes durable. Closing the connection without doing so leaves an open transaction; per the JDBC spec this is driver-defined, but the overwhelmingly common and recommended-safe behavior is an implicit rollback — so relying on "it'll commit anyway" is a real bug waiting to happen. Always explicitly commit() or rollback() in a finally/try-with-resources.

items.title: Unique constraint violation
items.context:
stmt.executeUpdate("INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES ('a@x.com')");
stmt.executeUpdate("INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES ('a@x.com')"); // email has a UNIQUE constraint

questions.prompt: What happens on the second insert?
choices: Overwrites the first row
Throws SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException (a subtype of SQLException)
Silently ignored, no row inserted
Throws IllegalStateException
questions.explanation: A UNIQUE constraint violation at the database level surfaces to JDBC as SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException, a specific SQLException subclass (the exact vendor error code varies, but this subclass is standard across compliant drivers). Frameworks like Spring translate this further into DataIntegrityViolationException in their own exception hierarchy.

items.title: Multi-resource JDBC try-with-resources order

questions.prompt: In what order are these three resources closed?
choices: PreparedStatement, then ResultSet, then Connection
Connection, then PreparedStatement, then ResultSet
ResultSet, then PreparedStatement, then Connection
All three close simultaneously
questions.explanation: try-with-resources always closes resources in the reverse of their declaration order. Declared as Connection, PreparedStatement, ResultSet, they're closed as ResultSet first, then PreparedStatement, then Connection last — which is also the logically correct order (close the most "dependent" resource first).

items.title: Partial failure in a JDBC batch update

questions.prompt: What is likely to happen when executeBatch() runs?
choices: All three inserts succeed regardless of the NOT NULL constraint
Compile error
It throws BatchUpdateException, and depending on the driver, the valid statements may or may not have already been executed
It silently skips the invalid statement and executes the other two
questions.explanation: When one statement in a batch fails a constraint, JDBC throws BatchUpdateException. Its getUpdateCounts() tells you which statements in the batch succeeded before the failure — behavior on whether later statements in the batch still run varies by driver (some abort immediately, some continue). This partial-failure ambiguity is exactly why batch error handling needs care in production code.

items.title: Optimistic locking version conflict

questions.prompt: What happens when transaction A tries to commit its update?
choices: Nothing — @Version is purely informational
It merges both transactions' changes automatically
It overwrites B's change silently — last write wins
JPA throws OptimisticLockException because the version A holds (5) no longer matches the row's current version (6)
questions.explanation: @Version implements optimistic locking: every update checks that the row's current version still matches what was read, and bumps it on success. Since B already advanced the row to version 6, A's UPDATE ... WHERE version = 5 matches zero rows, and JPA/Hibernate detects that and throws OptimisticLockException rather than silently letting A clobber B's change.

items.title: MongoDB unique index violation

questions.prompt: What happens on the second insertOne() call (MongoDB)?
choices: Throws SQLException
Overwrites the existing document
Silently ignored
Throws a DuplicateKeyException (error code 11000)
questions.explanation: A unique index in MongoDB rejects a second document with an equal indexed value, and the driver surfaces this as a DuplicateKeyException wrapping MongoDB's E11000 duplicate key error — the NoSQL equivalent of a relational UNIQUE constraint violation, just via a different exception type since there's no SQLException hierarchy involved.

items.title: SQL injection via string concatenation

questions.prompt: What is the effect of building the query this way with untrusted userInput?
choices: It throws SQLException because of the extra quote
It's safe as long as the column is indexed
JDBC automatically escapes string concatenation
It's vulnerable to SQL injection — the crafted input changes the query's logic to match every row
questions.explanation: String-concatenating untrusted input directly into SQL lets the input redefine the query's structure. With userInput = "' OR '1'='1", the query becomes ...WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1', a condition that's true for every row — a classic SQL injection bypassing whatever WHERE clause was intended. PreparedStatement with bound parameters (setString, not concatenation) prevents this because the driver sends the value separately from the SQL text.
